note: The paper argues that combining cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence now makes computer tutors as effective as human tutors, showing working systems for geometry proofs and LISP programming, which matters because it grounds AI in education in tested learning theory.
title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems
authors: John R. Anderson, C. Franklin Boyle, Brian J. Reiser

reading.body:
A 1985 paper claiming computer tutors can match human tutors has drawn 3,132 citations, making it one of the most cited works in AI in education.

The claim rests on two working systems, one for geometry proofs and one for LISP programming, built on the ACT theory of cognition. The argument is not that software teaches well in general but that grounding instruction in a tested model of how people learn is what closes the gap with human tutors. That distinction has held up: the paper is cited far more than most education technology work from its decade.

For AI specifically, the paper locates the difficulty in the cognitive model rather than the machine. The tutors work because the underlying theory specifies what a student knows and where that knowledge breaks, which is the same problem current systems face when they try to adapt to a learner. The data does not say how large the studies were, how the tutors compared against human tutors on measured outcomes, or whether the results replicated outside those two domains. It also gives no cost, hardware, or deployment figures, so it cannot speak to whether such tutoring scales.

explain_beginner: This paper says that computers can now teach students as well as human tutors can. The authors built tutoring programs using ideas from psychology about how people learn. One program helped students with geometry proofs, and another helped them write computer programs in LISP. The paper argues that combining thinking research and artificial intelligence makes this possible. This matters because it shows computer tutors can be grounded in tested learning theory, not just guesswork, so students might get effective teaching from machines.
explain_business: This paper indicates that computer-based tutoring can now match human tutors in effectiveness. The authors built working tutors for geometry proofs and LISP programming, using principles from cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence. For decision makers, this means investing in AI tutoring systems grounded in learning theory could deliver quality instruction at scale, potentially reducing reliance on human tutors for certain subjects. It informs choices about where to apply AI in education and supports prioritizing tools built on validated cognitive models rather than ad hoc software.
explain_practitioner: The authors argue that cognitive psychology, artificial intelligence, and computer technology have matured enough to build computer tutors matching intelligent human tutors. They developed tutors based on pedagogical principles from the ACT theory of cognition. These systems were built for two domains: teaching students to do geometry proofs and teaching them to write LISP programs. The key result is that such tutors are feasible and effective, demonstrating that grounding instructional design in a cognitive theory can produce working tutoring systems for real tasks.
